title: Free lord, dutiful servant
hook: Luther's Freedom of a Christian: free through faith, servant through love
tomorrow: what goes first on a list of things you got wrong?

segments.voice: Yesterday Luther began the morning with thanks for a night nobody guarded. Yesterday's line: kept this night.

Volunteer hours get logged for the application. Favors get tracked in a quiet mental ledger: I helped you move, so you owe me a ride. Martin Luther opens a short book, The Freedom of a Christian, with two sentences that tear up the ledger. A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. Nobody's servant, and everybody's. He means both.
screen: `HOURS LOGGED, FAVORS TRACKED.` → `FREE LORD OF ALL.` → `SERVANT OF ALL.`

segments.voice: The question: why serve anyone, if nobody can make you? Luther finds his riddle in Paul: "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all." Free how? By faith, Luther says. A person is made right with God by trusting God's promise, not by a pile of good works, and nothing outside can take that away. Servant how? Through love. Someone with nothing left to earn can turn every work outward, toward the neighbor who needs it. His boldest picture: be a kind of Christ to your neighbor. Churches put faith and works into words differently: Lutherans follow Luther's way of saying it, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of faith and good works together, in their own terms. A neighbor tradition knows this servant too. In the Mishnah, in the sayings called Pirkei Avot, Antigonus of Socho teaches: don't be like servants who serve the master for the sake of a reward; be like servants who serve with no reward in view, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you. Shared ground: service that isn't payment. One honest difference: Luther's servant serves because faith in Christ has already set him free, and the service runs toward the neighbor. Antigonus speaks of serving the Master, God, directly, with the fear of Heaven upon you. Two traditions, each in its own words, and a servant who isn't keeping score.
screen: `FREE FROM ALL, SERVANT UNTO ALL.` · `FREE BY FAITH, SERVANT BY LOVE.` · `ANTIGONUS: SERVE WITHOUT REWARD.` · `ONE SERVANT, TWO REASONS.` · then, large: `FREE, AND SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who can't pay you back, or won't even notice: a tired neighbor, someone eating alone, someone in a care home. Write a short message offering one plain help, and use the sit to decide when to send it. If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name.
Free lord. Luther's name for a Christian set free by faith, who then, through love, becomes servant of all.
Hold on to this one: free, and servant, with nothing owed in either direction. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Lutherans read The Freedom of a Christian as a short summary of Luther's teaching on faith and love; Christians of other churches read it too, and speak of faith and works in their own terms.

fork.setup: you tutor a younger kid every week. his family can't pay, and he never says thanks. a friend asks, 'why bother? you get nothing.' what's Luther's answer?
options: fair point; service should at least be noticed.
nothing to earn is exactly what makes it free service.
keep going, because it earns your place with God.
fork.reveal: for Luther, faith has already set the Christian free, so every work can turn toward the neighbor, and it's free because it isn't payment.

original.note: Latin, from Luther's Latin text: a most free lord.

trapdoor: what you thought: freedom means owing no one anything.
what it means: Luther's free person has nothing to earn, and so is free to serve everyone.
what a scholar hears: he builds both halves from Paul, free from all men, yet servant unto all, and closes with being a kind of Christ to the neighbor.
guess: a Christian set free by faith, who serves all
a ruler who owes no one any duty at all
a master who keeps servants of his own

chat.says: helped nia's great-grandma eat lunch at hospice. she won't remember me tomorrow. does that make it pointless?
options: Not pointless. Luther's free servant has nothing to earn; Antigonus says serve with no reward.
Kind of. Service counts most when it's remembered and builds the friendship back.
It's worth it because it earns you credit with God, even if she forgets.
chat.meaning: Luther: free through faith, a servant through love. Pirkei Avot: serve not for the sake of a reward. Neither is keeping score.

v3 wisdom shape and the unity thread: one question (why serve, if nobody can make you?), Luther's answer, then a neighbor in its own words and source: Pirkei Avot 1:3, Antigonus of Socho, paraphrased (no public-domain translation on the validator's list): be not like servants who serve for a reward, but like servants who serve with no reward in view, and let the fear of Heaven be upon you. One honest difference: Luther grounds the service in a freedom already given by faith in Christ, turned toward the neighbor; Antigonus speaks of serving the Master, God, with the fear of Heaven. Never 'all the same', ranks neither. A Jewish reader should confirm the paraphrase and that the difference is fairly put.
